This document compares the five group models for life satisfaction
(`stflife`, 0--10) on the same test set: ordinal logit, OLS, Lasso, MARS and the
regression tree. The code is the same as in `scripts/08_compare_models.R`,
which saves the comparison tables and figure. This document does not write any
files.

To render it, run `01_clean.R` and `03_train_test_split.R` first, make sure the
prediction files of all models are in `outputs/predictions`, then
`quarto render scripts/08_compare_models_documentation.qmd`.

# Setup

The code runs from the repository root, so the paths are the same as in the
R scripts.

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
```

```{r packages}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
```

# Joining the predictions

Each model script saves its test predictions in `outputs/predictions`, with the
columns `idno`, `cntry`, `essround` and `pred_<model>`. The id is all three
columns together, because `idno` repeats between countries and rounds. The
simpler Lasso (one-standard-error rule, `pred_lasso_1se`) is only a check in
`05_lasso.R`, so it is not compared here.

```{r join}
key  <- c("idno", "cntry", "essround")
test <- readRDS("data/ess_test.rds")[, c(key, "stflife", "anweight")]
test$cntry <- as.character(test$cntry)

for (file in list.files("outputs/predictions", pattern = "_test\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)) {
  p <- read.csv(file)
  test <- merge(test, p[, c(key, grep("^pred_", names(p), value = TRUE))], by = key)
}

pred_cols <- grep("^pred_", names(test), value = TRUE)
pred_cols <- setdiff(pred_cols, "pred_lasso_1se")

# every model must predict all test rows, otherwise the comparison is not fair
stopifnot(nrow(test) == 2537, !anyNA(test[pred_cols]))
pred_cols
```

# Test set metrics

RMSE, MAE and R² are weighted with the survey weights (`anweight`), the same as
in the model scripts. R² is 1 − SSE / SST, where both sums are weighted.

```{r metrics}
metrics <- function(y, p, w) {
  c(RMSE     = sqrt(sum(w * (y - p)^2) / sum(w)),
    MAE      = sum(w * abs(y - p)) / sum(w),
    Rsquared = 1 - sum(w * (y - p)^2) / sum(w * (y - weighted.mean(y, w))^2))
}

score <- function(i) {
  sapply(pred_cols, function(m) metrics(test$stflife[i], test[[m]][i], test$anweight[i]))
}

estimates <- score(seq_len(nrow(test)))

performance <- data.frame(Model = sub("^pred_", "", pred_cols),
                          round(t(estimates), 3), row.names = NULL)
performance <- performance[order(performance$RMSE), ]
kable(performance, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Are the differences real?

The test set is one random sample, so small differences between models can be
chance. A paired bootstrap checks this: the test respondents are drawn again
with replacement 9,999 times, the same drawn respondents are used for all
models, and the metrics are computed again each time. For each pair of models,
the 95% interval of the difference shows how large the difference could be;
if the interval contains 0, the models may not really differ. Many pairs are
tested at once, so the p-values are adjusted with the Holm method.

```{r bootstrap}
B <- 9999
set.seed(2026)
n <- nrow(test)

boot_scores <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(3, length(pred_cols), B),
                     dimnames = list(rownames(estimates), pred_cols, NULL))
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  i <- sample.int(n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  boot_scores[, , b] <- score(i)
}

pairs  <- combn(seq_along(pred_cols), 2)
output <- list()

for (j in seq_len(ncol(pairs))) {
  a <- pairs[1, j]
  b <- pairs[2, j]
  for (k in rownames(estimates)) {
    difference      <- estimates[k, a] - estimates[k, b]
    boot_difference <- boot_scores[k, a, ] - boot_scores[k, b, ]
    ci <- quantile(boot_difference, probs = c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
    null_difference <- boot_difference - difference
    p_value <- (1 + sum(abs(null_difference) >= abs(difference))) / (B + 1)

    output[[length(output) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      Model_A = sub("^pred_", "", pred_cols[a]),
      Model_B = sub("^pred_", "", pred_cols[b]),
      Metric = k, Difference = difference,
      CI_lower = ci[1], CI_upper = ci[2], p_value = p_value)
  }
}

pairwise <- do.call(rbind, output)
pairwise$p_Holm <- ave(pairwise$p_value, pairwise$Metric,
                       FUN = function(p) p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))
pairwise$Significant <- pairwise$p_Holm < 0.05
```

Differences in RMSE are Model A minus Model B, so a negative difference means
that Model A has the smaller error.

```{r pairwise-rmse}
rmse_pairs <- subset(pairwise, Metric == "RMSE",
                     select = c(Model_A, Model_B, Difference, CI_lower, CI_upper, p_Holm, Significant))
rmse_pairs[, 3:6] <- round(rmse_pairs[, 3:6], 4)
kable(rmse_pairs, row.names = FALSE)
```

The figure shows the test RMSE of each model with its 95% bootstrap interval.
The intervals overlap a lot, because each one also includes the chance of the
test sample, which is the same for all models. The paired differences in the
table above remove this shared part, so they are used for the conclusions.

```{r figure, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7}
rmse_ci <- t(apply(boot_scores["RMSE", , ], 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))
ord     <- order(estimates["RMSE", ], decreasing = TRUE)

par(mar = c(5, 8, 2, 1))
plot(estimates["RMSE", ord], seq_along(ord), xlim = range(rmse_ci), pch = 16,
     yaxt = "n", xlab = "Test RMSE (weighted), 95% bootstrap interval", ylab = "",
     main = "Model comparison on the test set")
segments(rmse_ci[ord, 1], seq_along(ord), rmse_ci[ord, 2], seq_along(ord))
axis(2, at = seq_along(ord), labels = sub("^pred_", "", pred_cols[ord]), las = 1)
```

# Summary

All models were compared on the same test set of 2,537 respondents, using RMSE,
MAE and R² weighted with the survey weights. To test whether the differences
between models are larger than chance, we used a paired bootstrap: the test set
was resampled 9,999 times, the same resampled respondents were used for all
models, and the 95% interval of each pairwise difference was calculated;
p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Holm method. The
ordinal logit model had the lowest error (RMSE 1.770, R² = 0.387), followed
closely by OLS (1.782), Lasso (1.782) and MARS (1.784), while the regression
tree was clearly weaker (1.874, R² = 0.314). The tree was significantly worse
than every other model (adjusted p = 0.001), but the differences between the
four best models were small (at most 0.013 in RMSE) and none was statistically
significant (all adjusted p-values 0.33 or higher). The more flexible MARS and the penalized Lasso
therefore did not predict better than linear regression, in line with Oparina
et al. (2025), who found only moderate gains from machine learning in
predicting life satisfaction.
